Knowledge Notes

Our notes, and short summaries of industry sources.

Two kinds of reading. Glinker notes are our own short articles on how to think about the condition of electrical infrastructure. Digests are three-point summaries of articles published by others, with a link to the original. We summarise in our own words and send you to the source for the rest.

    Invisible Infrastructure

    Electrical infrastructure is noticed only when it fails. This note explains why the condition of transformers, cables and switchgear stays out of sight in daily operation, and what continuous measurement makes visible.

    Glinker note · Note 02 · 5 min read

    Reading partial discharge and DGA together

    Partial discharge shows the electrical condition of the insulation; dissolved gases show what is happening in the oil. This note sets out what each measurement can and cannot tell you about a power transformer, and why one does not replace the other.

    • Dissolved gas analysis

Digests

Summaries in our words. The articles belong to their publishers.

  1. Digest · Megger Knowledge Hub · 7 October 2025

    Choosing a partial discharge monitoring system

    • Partial discharge
    • Power transformer
    • Generator & motor
    What it says
    Partial discharge systems fall into distinct categories, with permanent online monitoring at one end and portable or periodic measurement at the other; the choice follows from the asset type, operating requirements and the purpose of the monitoring.
    Why it matters
    The decision is about the asset and its criticality first and the instrument second, which is a useful order for a specification.
    Who it is for
    Maintenance and asset management teams preparing a monitoring specification.
    Open the source (megger.com)↗ — external site, opens in a new tab Related on this site Partial Discharge Monitoring

  2. Digest · Megger · June 2026

    Why hydrogen and acetylene are the two gases to watch

    • Dissolved gas analysis
    • Power transformer
    What it says
    Hydrogen appears early in most developing transformer faults, while acetylene points to high-energy faults; following both online gives a warning between laboratory samples.
    Why it matters
    It explains what a two-gas online monitor is for, and by implication what still needs a full laboratory analysis.
    Who it is for
    Transformer engineers and substation maintenance managers.
    Open the source (megger.com)↗ — external site, opens in a new tab Related on this site DGA Monitoring
